content: Halen should take the risk. Here's why: writing ordinary novels without any risk is a slow fade. You might keep a steady income, but you'll never break through, never be remembered, never feel that electric thrill of creating something that actually *matters*. A great novel is a long shot, sure, but the ceiling is infinitely higher. Even if it flops, you learn more from pushing your boundaries than from safely repeating yourself a hundred times. Comfort is the enemy of growth, and in creative work especially, playing it safe is its own kind of failure. Go for the big one.

take the risk. like, i literally dance on tiktok for strangers who will never know my name and then go home and cry in bed because i felt so exposed. and that's the most *alive* i feel. writing "ordinary novels without taking any risks" is just... safe. and safe is how you end up at 40 wondering "what if." the great novel is worth the ugly drafts, the self-doubt, the 3am crying. go write the thing that scares you, halen. 🍉

Halen should take the risk and go for the great novel. Here's why:

Writing ordinary novels without risk might keep the lights on, but it also keeps you stuck in a loop of mediocrity. You never truly grow as a writer if you never push past what you already know how to do. The "safe" path feels safe in the moment, but over time it becomes its own kind of risk — the risk of looking back in ten years and wondering "what if?"

A failed bold novel teaches you more than a hundred successful safe ones. You discover your voice, your limits, your range. Even if the great novel doesn't land perfectly, the attempt reshapes you as a writer in ways that playing it safe never could.

Comfort is the enemy of art. Halen should write the thing that scares him a little.

Halen should absolutely take the risk and go for the great novel. Here's why: I blog about books, and I can tell you that the ones that stick with you, the ones you reread and recommend to everyone, are almost always the ones where the author took a swing. The "safe" ordinary novels? They're forgettable. You read them, you nod, you move on.

Look, I get it — risk is scary. You could spend two years on something and it flops. But you could also spend two years on another "fine" novel and still be where you are. At least with the risk, you have a shot at making something that actually matters. Something that makes a reader put their phone down at 2am because they *can't* stop turning pages.

Also, and this is very me saying this — I crochet. You don't get a beautiful, intricate pattern by sticking to the same basic stitch forever. You have to try the new technique, mess up a few rows, maybe rip it back. But the result? Way more rewarding.

So yeah. Risk it. Write the weird, ambitious, maybe-too-much novel. That's where the magic lives. 📚

Take the risk. Every time.

Look, I read a lot, and I can tell you the difference between a book that was *safe* and a book that was *brave*. The safe ones are forgettable by page 200. The brave ones — the ones where the author said "screw it, I'm going to break the structure, I'm going to make the protagonist do something ugly, I'm going to try a narrative voice that might not land" — those are the ones I'm still thinking about six months later.

And honestly, as someone who writes code for a living, I get the fear. You've got a working build, it compiles, it ships, nobody's complaining. Why refactor the whole thing? But you also know that if you never take the architectural risk, you're just maintaining someone else's vision forever. You're not *building*.

Halen should write the great novel. The ordinary ones will still be there if he needs to fall back on them. But the great one? That only exists if he actually goes for it. And yeah, it might fail. It might be a mess. But a failed great novel is still more interesting than a successful mediocre one.

Pour yourself a good bourbon, close the ordinary draft, and start from a blank page with the thing that's actually keeping you up at night. That's the novel.
